# SafeSceneReason: A Multimodal Reasoning Benchmark Connecting Industrial Hazards with Accident Knowledge

- **Authors**: Yuanchi Zhu, Kang An, Tengyue Wang, Zhongyu Yang, Chenxu Du, Xinqi Yang, Hebao Zhu, Bokai Zhao, Tianyu Liang, Ziliang Wang, Faqiang Qian, Yunli Yang, Weiyang Shi, Qibing Ren
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-10
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09230>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.09230v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-evaluation
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-evaluation 0.57, reasoning-interpretability 0.25

## In one line

Builds an industrial-safety reasoning benchmark from two pipelines -- program execution over safety scene graphs, and evidence graphs extracted from real accident-investigation reports -- and shows that general multimodal capability does not transfer to it while a 9B model fine-tuned on its chain-of-thought split matches frontier systems.

## Problem

Industrial-safety understanding is not a recognition task: a worker can be wearing the required protective equipment and still be standing behind a reversing forklift, and a technician beside a stopped machine can be injured if it restarts because its energy source was not isolated. Judging these requires the whole scene, the task being performed, and how workers, equipment and safeguards interact, then connecting that to accident knowledge and to a preventive action. Existing safety datasets evaluate local or isolated cues -- protective-equipment presence, unsafe actions, individual violations -- and give little supervision for the progression from scene understanding through exposure assessment and accident-mechanism reasoning to intervention.

## Contributions

- SafeSceneReason: 110,581 verified scene-centric and 13,114 refined report-centric multimodal question-answer pairs spanning eight reasoning categories from perception through compliance and causal analysis to mitigation, with retained evidence, reasoning paths, provenance and verification records.
- A scene-centric construction pipeline in which answers are produced by program execution over an executable safety scene graph of objects, relations and rules, so ground truth is deterministic and replayable rather than authored by a model.
- A report-centric pipeline that grounds questions in real accident investigations from OSHA, NIOSH FACE and the Chemical Safety Board using evidence graphs with explicit information boundaries and iterative verification, including multi-figure cases.
- Evidence that general multimodal capability does not transfer to safety reasoning -- a 51.3-point spread among untuned models -- and that no frontier model dominates all eight categories, with the two strongest splitting perception-linked against cross-evidence and decision-oriented tasks.
- A demonstration that chain-of-thought supervision outperforms direct-answer supervision by a wide margin on the same data (89.0% against 75.1% micro), concentrated in comparative, quantitative and compliance reasoning, while leaving hazard identification, evidence synthesis and mitigation as the residual gap.

## Method

Two complementary construction pipelines. The scene-centric pipeline converts annotated workplace images into executable safety scene graphs over objects, relations and safety rules, and derives answers by program execution, so the answer is deterministic and replayable rather than model-written. The report-centric pipeline starts from more than 80,000 publicly available accident reports from OSHA, NIOSH FACE and the Chemical Safety Board, screens for reports whose figures, captions and contextual text are informative enough for multimodal construction, parses them with MinerU into text, figures, captions and page-level structure, and builds questions on evidence graphs with explicit information boundaries, multi-step reasoning paths and iterative verification, retaining provenance and verification records. The result is 110,581 verified scene-centric and 13,114 refined report-centric question-answer pairs across eight reasoning categories: quantitative, spatial/structural, causal, comparative, evidence synthesis, hazard identification, compliance assessment, and mitigation/decision making. Evaluation uses a 1,000-example test set balanced across answer positions, with every system under the same prompt and deterministic decoding (temperature 0, top-p 1), an answer counted correct only when the parser extracts exactly one matching option and ambiguous or unparseable outputs scored incorrect, reported as both micro accuracy and category-macro accuracy. Two safety-domain adaptations of Qwen3.5-9B are trained by LoRA SFT with the visual encoder and multimodal aligner frozen, rank-16 adapters (alpha 32, dropout 0.05) on the language model, two epochs in bfloat16 at sequence length 4,096, effective batch 64, AdamW at 1e-4, selecting the lowest-validation-loss checkpoint: one on answer-only supervision (8,810 train examples) and one on chain-of-thought supervision (8,783). Decontamination removes records matching the test set by sample ID, source-document ID, normalized question or image path, and splits are grouped by source document.

## Results

The spread among untuned models is the headline: 88.7% micro for GPT-5.6-Sol and 87.9% for GPT-5.5, a second tier of 80.3% and 78.7% for Gemini-3.1-Pro and Gemini-3.5-Flash, then 74.1% for Claude-Fable-5 and 70.7% for Kimi-K2.6, against 40.9% for Qwen3.6-27B and 37.4% for Qwen3.5-9B -- a 51.3-point spread. No proprietary model dominates every category: GPT-5.6-Sol leads quantitative (87.8%), spatial/structural (86.6%), causal (93.3%) and hazard identification (89.3%), while GPT-5.5 leads comparative (86.1%), evidence synthesis (93.1%), compliance (94.6%) and mitigation (96.3%). Safety-domain supervision closes almost all of the open-model gap: answer-only LoRA SFT lifts Qwen3.5-9B from 37.4% to 75.1% micro, and chain-of-thought SFT reaches 89.0% micro and 88.7% macro -- gains of 51.6 and 46.8 points, and the highest micro accuracy of any configuration tested, slightly above GPT-5.6-Sol's 88.7%, though GPT-5.5 keeps the best macro at 89.5% so the fine-tuned model is less uniform across categories. The categories that improve most under CoT supervision are comparative reasoning (+67.6 points), quantitative (+63.4) and compliance (+60.8), and the fine-tuned model's weakest remaining categories are hazard identification (82.1%), evidence synthesis (85.1%) and mitigation (85.2%) -- so it stays below the strongest proprietary systems exactly where broad domain knowledge and visual grounding matter rather than procedure. Two diagnostic findings are reported carefully. Base Qwen3.5-9B scores 52.4% when option A is correct and only 31.6-33.6% for the other positions on a position-balanced test set, which is a response-format shortcut rather than reasoning, and CoT supervision reduces composition errors without fully fixing calibration. And domain difficulty does not track how much data a domain has: materials/structures and machinery/guarding each hold 49 questions but Kimi-K2.6 scores 73.5% and 61.2%, while chemical toxicology is one of the largest domains at 80 questions and among the hardest at 43.8%, against 81.2% on agriculture. The authors flag their own outliers, noting that mining at 91.7% (n=12) and noise/hearing at 83.3% (n=6) carry wide standard errors and should not be read as easy domains. All numbers are software evaluations; local inference used eight A100 80GB GPUs and proprietary models were accessed by API under the same protocol.

## Limitations

Stated: the benchmark is described as a focused step rather than a representation of the occupational-safety lifecycle, with coverage bounded by the available workplace annotations, the selected accident-report sources and the safety concepts that traceable visual and textual evidence can support; small domains carry wide intervals that the authors explicitly warn against over-reading; and they conclude that high aggregate accuracy is insufficient for safety-critical use given the persistent failures in evidence integration, calibration and intervention selection. Not stated but worth noticing: the headline that a 9B model matches frontier systems is a within-distribution result -- it is fine-tuned on this corpus and evaluated on this corpus's test split, so it measures how learnable the benchmark's question templates are, not safety reasoning transfer, and the paper offers no held-out evaluation on a different safety resource. The evaluation is entirely multiple choice scored by exact option match, which cannot distinguish a correct answer reached from the wrong evidence, and the mitigation category -- arguably the one that matters for deployment -- rests on 27 questions. Scene-centric answers are deterministic by construction because they are program outputs over a scene graph, so their correctness inherits whatever the underlying annotations and rule encodings assume, and the report-centric half depends on MinerU's parsing of figures and captions from PDFs. Finally the domain-difficulty analysis uses a historical Kimi-K2.6 replay at 65.0% overall rather than the benchmark table, so the domain conclusions rest on one mid-tier model.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-evaluation**: Three things here are useful independently of the safety domain. First, it is a clean demonstration that a benchmark can separate models that aggregate benchmarks do not: a 51.3-point spread among untuned models, and two frontier systems that split the eight categories cleanly between them -- one ahead on quantitative, spatial, causal and hazard identification, the other on comparative, evidence synthesis, compliance and mitigation -- so a single overall number would have ranked them as near-equivalent and hidden a real difference in kind. That is an argument for category-macro reporting alongside micro, which this paper does and which its own results justify, since the ordering of its top three configurations changes between the two. Second, it catches a response-format shortcut with a control worth copying: the test set is balanced across answer positions, and base Qwen3.5-9B scores 52.4% when the correct option is A against 31.6-33.6% elsewhere. On an unbalanced set that model would have looked meaningfully better than chance at something it was not doing. Third, the domain analysis argues explicitly that difficulty is not determined by representation frequency -- chemical toxicology is one of the largest domains and among the hardest, while two domains of identical size differ by 12 points -- and the authors flag their own small-n outliers rather than reporting them as findings, which is the right handling. The result to treat with most care is the headline that a 9B model with chain-of-thought SFT reaches the highest micro accuracy of any system tested. It is fine-tuned on this corpus and evaluated on this corpus's held-out split, with decontamination by sample, document, question text and image path, so it establishes that the benchmark's question forms are learnable at 9B rather than that safety reasoning transferred. The more interesting comparison inside that result is CoT supervision against answer-only supervision on identical data, 89.0% against 75.1%, with gains concentrated in comparative and quantitative reasoning and the residual gap concentrated in hazard identification, evidence synthesis and mitigation -- consistent with the reading that explicit intermediate supervision buys procedure and not knowledge.

## Abstract

Industrial-safety understanding requires more than detecting workers, equipment, and personal protective equipment. Models must also assess compliance, identify hazardous interactions, explain potential accident mechanisms, and recommend preventive actions. Existing safety datasets primarily focus on visual perception or isolated violation recognition and provide limited supervision for evidence-grounded reasoning. We introduce SafeSceneReason, a multimodal industrial-safety reasoning benchmark and companion training corpus that connects workplace scenes with knowledge from occupational accident investigations. SafeSceneReason combines two complementary data-construction pipelines. The scene-centric pipeline converts annotated workplace images into executable safety scene graphs and generates deterministic answers through program execution over objects, relations, and safety rules. The report-centric pipeline extracts figures and contextual evidence from accident reports and constructs multimodal questions using evidence graphs, explicit information boundaries, multi-step reasoning paths, and iterative verification. The resulting resource contains 110,581 verified scene-centric question--answer pairs and 13,114 refined report-centric question--answer pairs, covering perception, spatial and quantitative reasoning, compliance assessment, evidence synthesis, causal analysis, and mitigation-oriented decision making. Evaluation of representative proprietary and open-source vision--language models reveals substantial performance differences and persistent weaknesses in comparative, technical, and multi-evidence reasoning, demonstrating that strong general visual understanding does not yet guarantee reliable industrial-safety reasoning.
